seal.statement: Lagrange has no committed Raft membership: liferaft's join and leave edit a local in-memory peer array whose quorum is computed from that array, each node reconciles its own array from cached service rows, a SYNCING row is a voter, no generation records the configuration, and term and vote are never persisted, so a restarted replica returns at term 0 free to vote again in a term it already voted in - all measured on the real production owners and reconfirmed at every round of the exhausted evaluation. That evaluation delivered findings but never certified its receipts; what justifies this work is that three independent adversarial verifiers each drove the raft-rs core themselves and each concluded the consensus core viable, the WASM RawNode boundary viable with named gaps, and migration undetermined with no decisive incompatibility. This quest is the experimental integration that turns that into evidence at the real Lagrange boundary, and it is not a production cutover. Behind the existing provider seam, selected explicitly by configuration and never silently the default, it runs fresh clusters on the raft-rs RawNode core over the existing Lagrange transport and real durable storage, with liferaft untouched, its logs unmigrated and its behaviour unchanged. Persistence comes first: a production-shaped Ready and apply loop whose order is derived from raft-rs 0.7's own documented host contract, durably preserving log entries, the hard state's term, vote and commit, applied progress, the configuration state and snapshot state, recording the commit index with or before applying committed entries, writing the configuration state and its applied progress atomically wherever recovery correctness requires them to agree, and reconstructing a restarted replica from its own durable Raft record with nothing inferred from a service or system-table cache. Then the central experiment: the core's configuration state is the authority for consensus membership and Lagrange rows project it outward rather than deriving it, proved against the liferaft case that started this - two peers whose caches disagree, one holding a still-syncing replica the other has never seen, must both observe the membership the committed configuration determines, and no cache mutation may alter quorum membership. Around the core it puts a safety boundary that validates what the host can know authoritatively - group and partition identity present, the recipient local, the envelope well formed, cross-group delivery unable to reach the core, corrupt encoding refused - without reproducing Raft's own checks and without the rule a verifier falsified, that a sender absent from the receiver's applied configuration may be refused, which rejects legitimate membership-transition traffic; whichever hostile messages still reach a trap are enumerated rather than hidden. A trap marks its runtime unhealthy, so the host stops dispatching into it, instantiates a fresh one and restores its groups from durable state, measured at real scales on real storage rather than against the evaluation's figures, in one runtime holding many groups with no sharding subsystem built in advance. It holds peer identity to a mapping that survives restart, ignores address, never follows list position, is never reassigned after retirement and crosses the JavaScript boundary exactly; it keeps a peer that is no longer a voter from participating in an election as though it were one, and settles pre-vote and check-quorum by running failure scenarios rather than by assumption; it leaves the judgment of whether a learner has caught up with Lagrange and the safe commitment of the change with the core; it drives the sequential add-learner, catch-up, promote and remove workflow through formation and recovery while keeping joint support tested; it exposes an explicit membership-change-in-progress result at the provider boundary instead of recreating a compatibility budget, with the core remaining the authority on whether another change can take effect; it establishes the snapshot and compaction contract now rather than after a cutover, so that configuration state and applied state never diverge across a restore; and it adds to the existing durable replica operation only the fields an integration falsifier proves necessary, with no separate transition subsystem and no speculative reason or generation fields. Every scenario runs on both backends and their application-level outcomes and safety properties are compared, without demanding identical internals and without preserving liferaft behaviour where that behaviour is itself the measured defect. It keeps a complexity ledger, because a backend that adds a mechanism while leaving every local membership machinery active is not a successful outcome, and it names precisely what can disappear after a cutover without deleting it here. Its result is one migration decision from a closed set - recommend cutover, continue experimental with named blockers, or reject with a named incompatibility - derived from what the scenarios measured, and a positive result is not forced.

text: Phase 1 (seam, binding, durable Ready loop, restart) by an Opus implementer under the lead's brief; receipts 1-6 of 24 green, 7-24 red because their witnesses do not exist yet. The seam: selectRaftBackend returns a named {backend, source} state, default liferaft by name and never by truthiness, an unknown or non-string name refused rather than defaulted, both backends imported in one file with no registry or dynamic import; the only production edit outside the new modules is one line of partition-service-core-base.js. The seam's real shape, derived by parsing src now rather than taken from the exhausted evaluation: 10 provider methods, and the node object createNodeClass returns carries 20 methods, 33 properties and 27 events - the evaluation's 'eleven MUST SERVE names' was a boundary error, since four are provider names and seven live on that node object, so a backend satisfying the provider seam must still produce a LifeRaft-shaped node. Phase 1 serves four provider names from the core and defers six, each refusing by name with its reason, and a test asserts served and deferred partition the derived census exactly. The binding is vendored at src/raft/raft-rs-wasm because production cannot import from test; its wasm and glue digests are byte-identical to the tagged rejected tree and the loader refuses a mismatch; the Rust was not rebuilt; raft 0.7's cited sources are vendored beside it with per-file digests, verified against the crates.io checksum, so every citation resolves from the repository. The loop iterates the contract rather than keeping an order of its own: twelve steps each citing raft-rs 0.7, with the documented contradiction recorded - lib.rs numbers committed entries third and hard state fifth and the example follows it, while the safety note at lib.rs:304-310 forbids that order and governs here - and a test reads the example's own line positions to confirm the contradiction is real. Storage is the replica's existing SQLite database in its own tables, chosen so that the configuration state and its applied progress share a transaction domain and are written by one statement; liferaft's tables are untouched and the restart test proves coexistence by poisoning them in the same file; every 64-bit value crosses as a decimal string bound as BigInt and nothing in the store passes through a JavaScript Number. Restart reconstructs term, vote, commit, applied, configuration state and the whole exported state equal to the live core's pre-crash reads and to an independent read-only connection to the file; the no-cache claim is structural, from the restore path's parameter names and its entire static import closure with a positive control, and behavioural, by poisoning liferaft's state, liferaft's log and a services row claiming other peers in the same database. METHOD DISCLOSURE by the implementer: production was written before the tests, so test-first ordering is not claimed; the falsification signal is an eight-mutant pass, all eight caught, two of them permanent host-fault subclasses that stand as standing falsifiers, and receipt 3's oracle is the core's own refusal captured live (raft_log.rs:314 applied out of range). Liferaft unchanged: zero diff on its five files, 73 of 73 raft test files and 105 of 105 partition test files green, and a seam-built and directly-built provider driven over the whole census surface produce identical effect traces. Two design debts recorded not resolved: createNodeClass is deferred, so the LifeRaft-shaped node object - the real integration surface - is untouched; and the provider's term and committed-index getters narrow a u64 to a Number and refuse past the safe integer rather than changing the seam's shape. Undriven and recorded as such: pre-vote and check-quorum are off and not chosen, no snapshot was produced, and the complexity ledger records nothing for this landing.

Lead decision on the fence conflict phase 1 surfaced. The vendored generated glue src/raft/raft-rs-wasm/pkg/raft_wasm.js (963 lines of wasm-pack output) breaks repository-wide checkers that walk src: eslint reports 851 style and no-undef errors, and the source oversized-file count goes from the 27 baseline to 28 on that one file. Two options existed: add each checker's own exclusion for the vendored artifact, or move the binding out of src, which would leave production importing a build artifact from outside the source tree with no existing vendor convention to hold it - the repository has neither a vendor nor a third_party directory. I authorise the exclusions, because a wasm-pack artifact is generated material no human maintains, this is the mechanism each checker already provides for exactly that, and it matches the precedent the exhausted evaluation set on the test side; no baseline is raised anywhere, and if a checker cannot express an exclusion without raising one the implementer stops and reports rather than raising it. The hand-written adapter stays ordinary source and is lint-clean. The alternative remains cheap to take later if the owner prefers generated material out of src entirely: the binding is one directory and the loader already refuses a digest mismatch, so moving it is a path change plus a vendor convention. Recorded so the owner can overrule without unpicking anything. Also recorded from phase 1 for the later phases: the seam's true integration surface is not the provider's ten methods but the LifeRaft-shaped node object createNodeClass returns, with twenty methods, thirty-three properties and twenty-seven events, which phase 1 deferred rather than shimmed; and the provider's term and committed-index getters narrow a u64 to a JavaScript Number and refuse past the safe integer rather than changing the seam's shape, which is an R08 tension left open, though Raft peer ids never pass through them.

Phase 2 (checker fence, ConfState authority, projections, ingress, hostile-message enumeration, trap handling) by a second Opus implementer under a written handover; receipts 7-11 green, probe 18 to 13, receipts 12-24 left red as instructed. Every test was written and run before its production module existed, with the failing output recorded - the method deviation phase 1 disclosed is not repeated - and six falsifiers were caught, including the verifier's exact fail-open finding and the falsified sender rule put into production deliberately to prove the receipt refuses it. Task 0 cleared the fence the lead authorised: five files, each through the checker's own exclusion mechanism, every baseline unchanged and now met exactly (eslint's ignores; a generated-artifact pattern beside the existing segment pattern in the file-size checker; ignorePatterns in both complexity checkers; knip's ignore). Checkers measured and left alone because the artifact does not cause them: unused:prod, deps, duplication, shards, scoped metrics. Receipt 7, the primary acceptance test: the part A case driven on the raft-rs backend with hostile per-peer caches rewritten between every settle round, node A's rows saying one thing and node B's saying another with a SYNCING row where liferaft counts a voter; all three peers report the same committed voters and the joiner is a learner on every peer's configuration, and the oracle is each peer's durable record read on an independent read-only SQLite connection, written from apply_conf_change's own return, never a literal and never the core compared with itself, with the cache-decided answer shown to differ so the check discriminates. Receipt 8: rows project and never alter - a hostile row edit promoting the learner, inventing a peer and deleting a voter leaves the exported configuration deep-equal on all three peers, a fresh proposal still commits, re-projection restores the committed configuration, the lifecycle column survives untouched and is never membership, and structurally the projection takes only core and handle while its class body cannot reach any mutating primitive, with a positive control proving the structural check can fail. Receipt 9: the admission function takes no core and no handle, so the receiver's applied configuration is unreachable by construction; the accepted type ranges are read out of the binding's own match arms; twelve malformed or misrouted shapes are refused by name and none reaches step, including the missing group id that the round-3 verifier found failing open; no refusal name mentions membership; and the membership race is driven live - a new voter added while a peer is partitioned, that peer healed and never ticked - giving zero refusals and the returning peer's commit advancing to the leader's, where the falsified rule as a control refuses the traffic and the entry never commits. Receipt 10: the shape list is parsed out of the owner's own direction document so a sentence without a driving shape fails the test, each shape runs in its own process, and three still trap with correct routing - an impossible heartbeat commit, a follower ReadIndex, and a contiguous-prefix non-contiguous append at the next Ready. Two departures from the round-3 report, measured here rather than cited: an empty ReadIndex to a leader did not trap although the test asserts the recipient was leading, and the follower trap is caused by term being set on the message rather than by the empty entries. Receipt 11: a trap moves the runtime to unhealthy, dispatch is then refused for every group by name and not only the group that trapped, replacement builds a genuinely new instance by dropping the glue's module cache, all three groups restore from real SQLite records equal to the durable bytes on an independent connection, and the restored groups are then driven - electing, committing a proposal, and committing and applying a configuration change verified durable on every peer's disk. Recorded undriven: pre-vote and check-quorum remain off and unchosen, no snapshot was produced, the complexity ledger records nothing, and the ingress boundary and runtime host are wired into the deterministic driver but not yet into the provider seam or the real transport. Phase 2 contributed no unused exports, de-exporting its own three and consuming one of phase 1's.

Lead decision on the unused-export ratchet phase 2 left red at 1447 against a baseline of 1438. This is not an owner decision: the steering entry point states that ratchet baselines are one-way and that the answer is to fix, de-export, extract or simplify rather than raise them, and phase 2 correctly refused to raise it. The nine excess exports are all phase 1's own hand-written modules - RAFT_RS_CORE_PRIMITIVE, RAFT_RS_TABLE, emptyConfState, fromExactInteger, toExactInteger, RAFT_RS_CRATE, RaftRsGroupHandle, runReadyCycle and the test driver's ClusterPeer - and phase 2 declined only because it was told not to edit phase 1's work. Phase 3 de-exports each one that no other module consumes and keeps those a later phase genuinely needs by consuming them there, so the ratchet is green before anything lands; no baseline moves. Recorded because the ratchet being red means nothing in this quest can land at all until it is cleared.

Phase 3 (ratchet, the node object, peer identity, election safety) by a third Opus implementer under a written handover; receipts 13, 14 and 15 added, probe 13 to 10, receipts 12 and 16-24 left red. Every test was written and run before its production module existed, with the failing output recorded, and real intermediate reds are reported rather than smoothed. Task 0: the unused-export ratchet is green at 1438 of 1438 with no baseline raised - eight de-exported and one closed by phase 3 consuming it. The implementer also found the literals gate already red at 110 violations from phases 1 and 2, added 10 of its own, and cleared all 120 without raising a baseline, giving the vendored binding the checker's own skip mechanism and moving seven hand-written literals to their constants owners; the lead reviewed this and accepts it as the same class as the recorded fence decision. The node object: every census member is present and answered in exactly one of three named ways - served from the core, deferred, or never applicable - with the partition asserted disjointly against the census derived from src, so an absent member cannot read as undefined and take a quiet path. Three judgments worth the owner's eye: the role vocabulary consumes LifeRaft's own constants by reading them off the class so a copy cannot drift, while raft-rs's fourth role PreCandidate is deliberately given a value outside that enum rather than mapped onto CANDIDATE, which would be the imitation that silently lies; term and leader are served for reading and refuse the write by name, because production writes both on a liferaft node and under this backend they are the core's; and nodes is a read-only projection of the committed configuration whose entries refuse any field beyond address, peer id and learner. Wired into production and not only into a driver: the node's real inbound path runs the envelope boundary, then step, then the Ready drain, then emits role and commit events off the core's own status, with a misrouted envelope refused by name and the core's status byte-identical across the refusal; every core call goes through the runtime host, so a trap marks the runtime unhealthy in src and every node in that runtime, not only the one that trapped, then refuses dispatch. THE SEAM FINDING, which section 2 of the direction anticipated and the lead verified independently: selecting the raft-rs backend does not change the node a partition runs on, because partition-service-raft-init-base.js:408 constructs class RaftNode extends LifeRaft directly and never calls the provider's createNodeClass - whose only callers in src are the message-group and replica-base paths; four modules under src/partition additionally compare against the concrete LifeRaft enum, the seam's context carries an address resolver and a packet writer but none of the durable store, group id, peer id, starting configuration or tick schedule a raft-rs group needs, and the partition lifecycle wiring subscribes to a liferaft-internal commit-rollback event the raft-rs node refuses. The node was built anyway because it is the right boundary for the message-group path and it is what makes ingress and runtime health real in production, but a partition-level experiment needs an owner change at that construction site. Receipt 13: identity is a digest of the logical replica identity masked to 63 bits, recorded in a durable table, proved stable across a close and reopen, independent of address structurally with a positive control, order-independent against the existing list-position mapper measured giving different ids under two orders, never reassigned after retirement with the refusal re-proved after closing the registry and reading the row on an independent connection, exact above the safe integer with the same value through a JavaScript Number shown to differ, and driven through a real cluster where the core's own reported id matches the registry character for character. Receipt 14: a named refusal for learner, not-a-voter, core-not-promotable and retired-by-host, each measured, with the campaigned learner's effect reproduced without the guard so the guard is shown to prevent something; and the case the configuration rules cannot see is measured rather than hidden - a peer removed while partitioned still holds a configuration listing itself, is admitted by those rules, and when ticked disturbs the cluster, with only the host's own durable retirement record refusing it, which makes the invariant about withholding ticks rather than withholding an explicit campaign. Receipt 15: pre-vote and check-quorum settled by failure scenarios, each judged only against the run differing in that setting alone after a first derivation proved non-deterministic between runs; both reach the core, pre-vote measured by raft-rs's own PreCandidate role and zero terms burned against five or six, check-quorum by an isolated leader standing down at round ten instead of believing it leads for ninety, at a cost of one extra round to restabilise; the recommendation is derived from those runs rather than stored, and the tuning defaults were deliberately not flipped because every earlier receipt was measured with them off. Verification state: 73 of 73 raft and 105 of 105 partition test files green, liferaft's five files zero diff, all ratchets green and none raised. No independent verifier has attacked any of this.

Phase 4 (gates, the partition construction seam, the apply-rollback contract) by a fourth Opus implementer under the owner's phase-4 addendum; four WIP checkpoints committed on the quest branch (b78229ce2, 66b5f63b5, f08862ea6, ac075aa5a), stopped after step 2 on budget with steps 4 and 5 not started. Gates: the staged-file literal check ignored the skip list because the shared collector consults it only on the directory branch and the hook passes explicit paths, so an explicitly named file is scanned regardless; fixed at the owner's cause rather than at the checker by moving the generated binding from src to vendor, after which SIX exclusions were removed and are byte-identical to the sealed base, with one honest root declaration left - vendor is declared non-source in eslint once, the way node_modules is, because the hook reaches eslint with explicit paths. The move surfaced a new eslint red on first commit and that too was fixed at the cause rather than by reinstating the subtree exclusion. No baseline raised anywhere; digest verification, pinned toolchain metadata and the vendored citation sources kept, and the package manifest now ships the vendor root. The decision-boundary violation was a raw null outcome in the ready loop, fixed by naming the outcome in its constants owner. Seam: a thirteen-field request names what a group hands its backend - group and peer identity, peer address, bootstrap peers, the durable log, timing, substrate, election deferral, the send and address hooks, the committed-entry applier, snapshot catch-up and the apply-rollback hook - not one a liferaft name and none a hidden global; createPartitionNode became a required provider-contract method that liferaft implements by translating into its own option names and returning the subclass that used to be declared inline at partition-service-raft-init-base.js:408, while the experimental backend answers the name by refusing it with its reason. src/partition no longer extends LifeRaft anywhere, verified by the lead. Parity measured, not asserted: 105 partition files and 2423 tests with zero failures, identical after step 2, plus targeted checks that the node the service runs on is identity-equal to what the provider returned, is a LifeRaft instance, and that its address, log, beat and election bounds equal the service's own state; one honest nuance is that a debug log moved marginally earlier, both branches of the override it sat in having only called the callback. Apply-rollback: what the lifecycle wiring consumed was exactly one fact, that the durable apply transaction did not commit, with one consequence, that the cached applied watermark may be ahead of the store; since every backend can fail an apply transaction that is a true partition requirement, so the fact crosses as a request hook while the event name does not, the wiring no longer imports the liferaft commit scheduler, and raft-rs is not made to emulate it. Deleted as dead: partition-raft-node.js and its constants, which had no production caller and sent packets down a different path from the live one - a stale divergent duplicate and the last direct subclass in src/partition - and the now-unused rollback wiring helper. NOT DONE and honestly unknown: whether a real partition survives restart, whether ConfState stays authoritative under hostile caches through the real partition path rather than the deterministic driver, and whether sequential learner promotion and removal work; retirement as scheduling eligibility is not started. No verifier has attacked any of this.

Interface reduction table, phase 4, derived from src (the thirteen members src/partition reads off its raft node). Retain as true or generic requirements: nodes, who is in the group, which must become a projection of the committed configuration; state, role observation, whose vocabulary must stop being LifeRaft's enum; leader; term; on and emit for lifecycle events and inbound ingress; setTickInterval, configureTickInterval and tickIntervalMs for tick control. Remove from the node surface: command, since proposing is already a provider method. Named liferaft implementation details to remove: change to force leadership on a single replica, since a one-voter configuration elects itself; deferCandidacy, which is the liferaft-shaped version of retirement as scheduling eligibility; and leave, a local membership mutation that must become a proposed configuration change. Surface size: before, a backend running a partition group had to BE a LifeRaft subclass, so eighty public members plus a nine-method provider contract; after, the required interface is ten provider methods, thirteen request fields and at most thirteen node members, thirty-six names, of which three are named for removal. The owner's stop condition did not fire - the facade is nowhere near LifeRaft's size - with the caveat stated plainly that for the liferaft backend the returned node still is a LifeRaft, so what shrank is the surface a backend is REQUIRED to provide, not liferaft's own. Remaining concrete LifeRaft dependencies in src: six enum reads (learner-promotion-proof, write-metrics-base, raft-init-base, three in transaction-base, plus raft-timing-utils and tracked-leader-demotion outside partition), the three liferaft-only calls above, and the re-export from partition-service-shared.

Two findings routed out of scope rather than absorbed (R17). One: the guideline checkers bypass their own skip list when given explicit file arguments - guideline-check-shared.js collectJavaScriptFiles consults shouldSkipDirectory only on the directory branch, so a path that stats as a file is returned unfiltered, which is how a generated file inside a governed root passed the skip list and failed the staged-file check. The owner's vendor move made it moot for this quest, but the hole is real for any future generated file under a governed root. Owner: guideline-audits. Not repaired here. Two: test/raft/liferaft-formation-attribution-interaction.test.js is red on main independently of this quest - three named subtests and ten assertions fail, confirmed pre-existing by re-running with this quest's work stashed at the first checkpoint; the rest of the raft suite is 87 files and 2069 tests with 2059 passing. Owner: whoever owns the formation attribution interaction; it blocks a whole-corpus green and therefore any publish.
